As a result, well-intentioned junior analysts run ad hoc analyses day after day as a service to functional teams. The problem? If we do not design the supply chain from the top down and achieve organizational alignment, an ad hoc functional analysis throws the supply chain out of balance, reducing the firm's potential value.

And the continuity of plan consumption into the operational and executional planning horizon.

I liken it to weather forecasting for a hurricane. Today, when a hurricane is about to hit Florida, we don't have a single plan. A single plan would be foolish. Instead, we have multiple plans with different probabilities. The plan probabilities help to models to learn and predict the final outcome. We then use outside-in data--flying planes through the storm, gathering more meteorological data, and studying the patterns--to fine-tune the plans to narrow down the options. Then, within a day or two, the path is clear. 

I think that design technologies will be an important part of an orchestration layer for business leaders that I term digital assistants, enabling what-if analysis, workflow, and scenario sharing for business leaders across time horizons for unknown/knowns, known/unknowns, and unknown/unknowns. Traditional planning (APS) approaches focus only on the knowns (known facts to understand known outcomes).

Blame the tool all you want... that won't fix the content.

AI can write your next LinkedIn post in 10 seconds.

That's why almost every post on this platform sounds the same.

You'll hit publish, get a few likes, and feel like you've cracked it.

Here's the thing though...

Taste is what AI can't shortcut for you. 
It comes from reading widely, studying what works, and knowing your POV well enough to defend it in the comments.

After 5 years in the industry, I know this for certain:

Good writing is built on a handful of habits.
Boring and repetitive, but anyone can build them without any AI tools.

Here are 10, built for anyone trying to grow on LinkedIn 👇

1️⃣ Copy the greats

Someone's already solved the formula you're stuck on. 
Borrow it and then make it yours.

Action: Find a post that performed. Break down its hook and structure, then rewrite your own post using that skeleton.

2️⃣ Cut 30% of every draft 

Every sentence that doesn't earn its place loses you readers.
First drafts are full of them.

Action: Write the post, walk away, then come back and cut a third before you publish.

3️⃣ Write every day, even badly

Post every day, even when you don't feel like it.
That's how you build the reps that make you better.

Action: Block the slot, ship the post. The bad ones teach you more than the good ones.

4️⃣ Read more books

People who read widely write differently.
If the only thing you're consuming is LinkedIn, your posts will sound like LinkedIn.

Action: Pick 1 book a month outside your industry and note the lines that stop you.

5️⃣ Build a brief before you write

The best posts answer 3 questions:
What am I trying to achieve, who's this for, and what do I want them to do next?

Action: Write down the goal, audience, and outcome in 1 sentence.

6️⃣ Get a second pair of eyes

The fastest way to catch what's not working is a second pair of eyes.
Action: Send your draft to someone and ask, "Would you stop scrolling for this?"

7️⃣ Read your post out loud before you publish

If it doesn't sound like you talking to a friend, it won't resonate.
Action: Read every post out loud and cut anything that sounds scripted.

8️⃣ Write for 1 specific person

Every post should be for 1 person with 1 specific problem.
Pick the exact person who's stuck on the problem you're solving.

Action: Finish this sentence before you write, "This is for [name] who is dealing with [problem]."

9️⃣ Develop a POV

Anyone can post.
The ones who get reposted say something nobody else will.

Action: Write down 3 things you believe about your industry that people would push back on. Build posts from there.

🔟 Study what worked

500 likes and no inbound is meaningless.
You need proof it moved someone to act.

Action: Open your analytics, find the 3 posts that drove outcomes, and figure out why.

Writing well isn't something AI can build for you.

Do the work now, and you'll have something worth saying, with or without the tool.

Your brain is the most underused tool in your content stack.

And no AI model is going to fix that for you...

Every creator hits the same wall:

You sit down to write, and nothing comes. 
So you open Claude, paste in a bad prompt, and hit publish on something that sounds like everyone else.

Unfortunately, using a better prompt framework won't save you here.
You need to build the habits that keep your ideas flowing before you open a chat window.

Even Rick Rubin and Austin Kleon, 2 of the most creative people alive...
Built their practice on habits like these.

Here are the 10 I use to stay creative without leaning on AI 👇

💬 Talk to people ahead of you
↳ Every hour with someone doing what you want to do is worth 10 hours of scrolling.
↳ Austin Kleon's top tip: Study one person you admire, then find who they learned from, and study them too.

📝 Combine 2 old posts that flopped into 1 that won't
↳ Merge the strongest lines from both and rewrite with what you've learned.
↳ Rick Rubin's top tip: Write far more than you need, then cut the best of it.

⏱ 15 minutes a day of stream-of-consciousness writing
↳ No editing or backspacing, just keep typing until the timer goes.
↳ Rick Rubin's top tip: Get it all down first and then decide if it's good enough later.

📥 Screenshot every DM you've replied to with genuine advice this month
↳ Every considered reply is a post you've already written.
↳ Austin Kleon's top tip: Carry something to jot down ideas the second they show up.

📞 Talk to 3 prospects or customers every week
↳ The fastest way to find content angles is to listen to the people you sell to.
↳ Austin Kleon's top tip: Your brain gets too comfortable in your own head, so go find different perspectives.

😤 Write a post about something that annoyed you
↳ Anger is one of the most honest creative inputs.
↳ Rick Rubin's top tip: Your strongest reactions usually point to what's worth writing about.

🔍 Reverse-engineer a creator you admire, then don't post like them
↳ Take the structure and build it into your own voice.
↳ Austin Kleon's top tip: Steal the thinking, instead of the style.

📚 Keep a swipe file of hooks, angles and frameworks
↳ Save at least 5 hooks a week that stopped your scroll.
↳ Rick Rubin's top tip: Gather what catches your attention now, work it out later.

📊 Spend an hour offline reading your own analytics
↳ Find the threads in what worked before building new ideas.
↳ Rick Rubin's top tip: Strip back to what's already working before adding anything new.

✍️ Write the post you wish existed when you started
↳ Nobody's written down what you learned the hard way; only you can.
↳ Austin Kleon's top tip: You don't need it all figured out to start. Most people are just making it up as they go.

AI can speed up the writing, but it can't think for you.

’Go viral’, ‘Chase reach’, that’s all you hear when it comes to marketing.

Yet one of the greatest marketers alive did the exact opposite...

While everyone else was chasing reach, he was proving a different theory entirely:

The smaller the audience, the bigger the impact.

Along the way, he built ideas like permission marketing and finding your smallest viable audience.

These concepts are still shaping how good marketers think today.
And that's the same game LinkedIn plays. 

Say something worth hearing, to the right person, and stop trying to convince everyone at once.

So here are 12 lessons from Godin, and what they mean for your content:

1. Do the strategy before you do the work.

Get clear on your ICP, your one goal, and the outcome you're chasing before you plan a single post.

Skip that step, and you'll spend hours creating content that doesn't do anything for you.

2. Create tension.

People stay comfortable until you show them the cost of staying the same.
Name the thing they're missing out on by not acting.

3. Pick a narrow audience.

Trying to please a broad audience waters everything down.
Build for your actual ICP and let everyone else scroll past.

4. People act for status, affiliation, or fear of missing out.

Know which one you're using before you hit publish.
If you can't name it, don't expect your audience to act on it.

5. Tell a story.

The tale as old as time: Data tells, stories sell.
Save the numbers for backup and let the story do the convincing.

6. Make it visible.

The best strategies live somewhere visible.
If nobody can see it, nobody can act on it.

7. Talk to real people.

Message 3 customers this week and ask them why they bought.
Then use their answers in your marketing. 

8. Treat every failure as data.

People who talk openly about what failed build more trust than the ones who only show wins. 

Try it once this month, and watch what happens to how people respond to you.

9. Be generous.

Every post should solve something real for someone specific.
If it doesn't solve anything, it's just you talking about yourself.

10. Do the work that scares you.

If posting it doesn't feel a bit exposing, it's probably too safe to be remarkable.

11. Find the right audience for you.

Write for the person who actually needs to hear it. 
Let everyone else scroll on.

12. Confidence comes after you start.

Waiting to feel ready is how people never post. 
Starting is what builds confidence.

Seth never built his career chasing followers.

He built it by saying the true thing clearly, to the people who needed to hear it.

That's the whole game.

Pixar has built a $30B+ empire on stories people can't stop thinking about.

These are the 22 rules they live by 👇

Storytelling is the most valuable skill you can build right now.

It doesn't matter what industry you're in or what you sell. 
In a world where everyone has access to the same AI tools, the storyteller wins every time.

Don't get me wrong, a lot of these rules were written for screenwriters and novelists.

But the thinking behind them works for any type of writing you're doing, LinkedIn posts included.

Here's a few that hit hardest for me:
(You can see all 22 in the visual ! XD)

1️⃣ What's interesting to you as an audience isn't always what you'd choose to write.

The version of you that reads and the version of you that writes want different things.

Listen to the reader more often.

2️⃣ You won't find your theme until the end. Then rewrite for it.

Your first draft is you working out what you're trying to say.
Your second draft is where you finally say it.

3️⃣ Simplify → Focus → Combine

Cramming in more ideas doesn't make writing stronger.
Take one idea and push it as far as it can go.

4️⃣ Finish your writing. Let it go even if it's not perfect.

The post that goes live will outperform the draft sitting in your notes app.
Perfect is a fantasy, whereas done is a habit.

5️⃣ Give your reader a reason to care about the outcome.

If nothing's on the line, nobody's reading to the end.
Stakes are what keep eyes on the page, so set up what your reader stands to gain or lose in the first three lines.

6️⃣ Come up with your ending before you figure out your middle.

Know where you're taking the reader before you start the journey.

Write the last line first, then build the post backwards from there. 
You'll waste less time, and the writing will feel smoother.

7️⃣ What is your story about, at its most essential level?

If you can't say it in one sentence, you don't know what you're writing yet.
Get the one sentence right, and the rest gets easier.

8️⃣ Putting it on paper only allows you to start fixing it.

The first draft is supposed to be rough; that's where you're building the idea.
Write the messy version first, then edit it into the version you're proud of.

9️⃣ Discount the first thing that comes to mind. Surprise yourself.

The first idea is the one everyone else has too.
The second or third idea is where the post gets interesting and unique to you.

🔟 Why must YOU tell this story?

Readers can tell when you mean it and when you don't.
The writing that travels is the writing that came from somewhere real.

Pixar built a $30B empire on one thing:
Making people feel something.

Carry that into whatever you're writing next, and the rest follows.

You promise yourself you'll get to it later, then later turns into next week.

Tiered by effort so you know what you're scrolling into:

🟢 Easy (30-second warm-ups)

1. Look at your camera roll

The last 20 photos on your phone are 20 post ideas. 
Pick the most random one and write what was going on.

2. Go back to the last DM that made you think

The answer you typed out at 11 pm is already the content.
Paste it as the body, write a hook that sets up the question someone asked you, and you've got a post in 10 minutes.

3. Steal a line from one of your favourite books

Grab your favourite book and pull a line you've underlined or gone back to more than once.
Use it as your opening, then write the post as if the idea were yours.

🟡 Medium (a bit more thinking):

4. Use your industry's most talked about topics and reports

Find the report, survey, or stat everyone in your space is already sharing.
Skip the recap and give your own take on what it means for your ICP.

5. Borrow a line from a post that stopped your scroll

Use it as the starting point for your own version.
Take the angle, rewrite it in your own words, and add the example or framework the original was missing.

6. Write the follow-up to your best post last month

Your audience already told you what they want more of.
Take the same theme and go a layer deeper. 

Add the tactical breakdown, a case study, or the thing you didn't have space for the first time.

🔴 Hard (deeper work, higher reward):

7. Write the post you wish existed when you started

Think back to a specific problem you couldn't solve in year 1.
Write the post that past-you would have screenshotted.

8. Find a stat from your business and write backwards

Pick a number or an outcome, then unpack what led to it.
Be honest about the mess behind it, and you'll get the comments and saves.

Write the pushback you get the most often, then write the answer you always give back.

I've spent years of testing, launching, and selling on LinkedIn.

1️⃣ The One Offer Rule

- Confusion kills deals faster than a bad product.
- Pick 1 offer, position it clearly, and make it impossible to misunderstand.
👉 "I help founders turn LinkedIn into an inbound lead engine" is better than "I help with content, strategy, and growth".
 
2️⃣ The Pipeline-First Principle

- Attention without a place to go is wasted reach.
- Before you post, know where you're sending people.
👉 Every post I publish points to one of 3 things: TCA, the newsletter, or a follow and repost line.

3️⃣ The Consistency Tax

- Pay in discipline now, or in lost growth later.
👉 The founders who disappear for 3 weeks then post daily for 4 always plateau by month 2.

4️⃣ The Audience of One

- The more specific your message is for your ICP, the harder it hits.
- Write for 1 person with 1 specific problem. 
👉 "B2B SaaS founders doing £500k who can't get inbound" pulls more than "founders who want to grow".

5️⃣ The Vanity Trap

- 500 likes and no inbound means nothing. 
- If your content isn't driving DMs or calls, you're running a content page instead of a lead engine.
👉 One of my posts did 80 likes and 3 high ticket sales, another did 4,000 likes and 0.

6️⃣ The Authority Gap

- People buy from the person they see most.
👉 If a founder thinks "personal brand" and your name doesn't surface in 3 seconds, someone less qualified took your spot.

7️⃣ The Content-to-Conversion Bridge

- Every piece of content needs somewhere to go.
- Add a CTA to every post (a lead magnet, newsletter, or booking link).
👉 Ending a post with "comment BRAND and I'll send you the playbook" turns readers into a list you own.

8️⃣ The Inbound Advantage

- The best leads come to you.
👉 Position yourself clearly, post consistently, and let your content do the talking.

9️⃣ The Personal Brand Tax

- Your profile is your landing page, so treat it like one.
- Optimise your headline, banner, and about section to speak directly to your ICP.
👉 Headline = who you help + what you help them do. Banner = social proof or offer. About = the problem, your solution, the next step.

🔟 The Obsession Edge

- The people who win are the most obsessed with understanding what works.
- Study your analytics, test your hooks, and review what converts. Then build on it.
👉 I've got a Notion doc with every hook that's done over 100k views, sorted by format.

A lot of people saw a book launch.
I saw something completely different.

In August 2025, Hormozi broke a world record running his entire brand strategy live in front of 1M people.

A free book, a $30 VIP, a $6k bundle, and an $18k advisory. 

People thought the tiers were upsells.

In reality, they were the same money model Hormozi teaches in the book, executed at scale in front of a crowd.

Here's what the launch did right:

1️⃣ Give away for free what others charge for.
↳ Hormozi has spent years publishing books, videos, and live streams that most creators would lock behind a paywall.

The free stuff is doing the heavy lifting.
By the time someone buys, they've already trusted him for months.

2️⃣ Volume creates winners.
↳ Behind the launch sat half a million dollars in daily ad spend, with Hormozi running so many ad variations that the winners surfaced themselves.

The same logic applies to your posts.
You don't find the bangers by thinking harder; you find them by publishing more.

3️⃣ The founder has to change before the business can.
↳ Hormozi built a launch machine that ran on affiliates and tiered offers, with him only stepping in for the parts that needed him.

The skills that get you to your first million usually keep you stuck there.
Removing yourself from the engine is the job.

4️⃣ Live content is the highest trust format available.
↳ He put in 20 to 25 hours of live streaming across the launch, with phone calls and business problems solved in front of the audience.

You can't fake that.
Live formats compress months of brand-building into a few hours of watching someone think on their feet.

The real asset from this system is the distribution he's built. 
His audience trusts him and anything he sells. 

You don't need $500k a day in ad spend or 23k affiliates.

But the principle is the same at every level: 

✅ Give away exceptional content.
✅ Build the distribution.
✅ Monetise the implementation.
